newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea central bank wants to keep supervisory role.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea central bank wants to keep supervisory role.

text.p: South Korea's outspoken central bank governor on Thursday threw himself into the fray over a proposed unified financial supervisory watchdog, arguing that the central bank should continue to supervise banks.
"I think it is not right to separate the role of bank supervision from the Bank of Korea," Lee Kyung-shick said in a statement on the bank's 47th anniversary.
"Without that function, the central bank, as the final lender, will lose much of its ability to prevent and manage financial crises," said Lee.
The central bank governor is known for speaking his mind.
Proposed reforms of rules governing the central bank should focus on guaranteeing neutrality and autonomy in establishing and implementing monetary policy, he said.
Earlier this month, a presidential commission studying financial reforms proposed that the banking, insurance and securities supervisory bodies be unified under the authority of the prime minister.
Currently, the three bodies report ultimately to the finance ministry, though the bank watchdog's immediate boss is the central bank.

The unified watchdog was just one of the commission's proposals, which generally would grant more autonomy to financial institutions, increase central bank independence and lift various government regulations.
The finance ministry is drafting implementing legislation, which is to be introduced to a special parliamentary session in June.
Analysts said the ministry stood to lose the most authority under the commission's proposals and was unlikely to sympathise with the central bank's request to retain its bank supervisory role.
"It's a political turf war," said Im Joon-hwan, a senior banking analyst at Schroders Securities.

"The finance ministry may gracefully give up its supervisory powers to erase its image of being too powerful and bureaucratic. But it has no intention of giving bank supervisory power to the central bank."
Analysts said the finance ministry probably supported the commission's idea of unifying the supervisory agencies.
Separately, the finance ministry and the Bank of Korea have been at odds over increasing central bank independence.
Analysts said the Bank of Korea had not proved itself as a supervisory authority.

"Although it would be desirable for a central bank to have both powers of monetary policy-making and bank regulating, the Bank of Korea doesn't have much of an argument because it hasn't exercised its supervisory power properly," said Brian Hunsaker, a banking analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
He said if the central bank had kept closer watch on banks, South Korea would not have experienced the financial turbulence sparked by a string of corporate collapses this year.
"It cannot be much of a big loss for the central bank," Hunsaker said.
